text: Hillsong Church, commonly known as Hillsong, is a charismatic Christian megachurch and a Christian association of churches based in Australia. The original church, Hills Christian Life Centre, was established in 1983 by Brian Houston and his wife, Bobbie Houston, in Baulkham Hills, New South Wales. Prior to this, in 1977, Brian Houston's father, Frank, founded the Sydney Christian Life Centre (Sydney CLC) in inner-city Sydney, described by scholar Sam Hey as "a neo-Pentecostal megachurch." Both Sydney CLC and Hills CLC were affiliated with the Australian Christian Churches (ACC), the Australian branch of the US-based Assemblies of God. Hills CLC grew into a megachurch in the 1980s and 1990s due to its contemporary worship music and international church planting strategy. In 1992, it planted London Christian Life Centre, later renamed Hillsong London, which expanded to twelve locations in the UK, and Kyiv Christian Life Centre, now Hillsong Kyiv, in newly independent Ukraine. In 1997, Hills CLC moved into a new building at Baulkham Hills' Norwest Business Park. The church merged with Sydney CLC in May 1999 after Frank Houston was exposed as a paedophile; Brian Houston served as senior pastor of both churches for eighteen months. The combined church was renamed Hillsong Church in 2001. Between 2008 and 2018, Hillsong planted churches in Russia, South Africa, Sweden, Israel, Canada, and Mexico, and established sixteen locations in the United States by 2022. In September 2018, Hillsong left the ACC—where Brian Houston had been national superintendent/president from 1997 to 2009—to become an autonomous denomination, citing practical reasons such as the ability to ordain pastors in Australia for legal weddings, while affirming no doctrinal shift and maintaining the ACC as their "tribe." At that time, the church had 80 churches. In October 2020, Hillsong purchased the Festival Hall in Melbourne for its weekly services; in October 2021, it bought the Golders Green Hippodrome in London for Sunday services. Brian Houston resigned as chairman of the Hillsong board in September 2021 due to pressures from a court case over his alleged failure to report his father’s sexual abuse of a child, which he became aware of in the 1990s. On 31 January 2022, Phil and Lucinda Dooley were announced as acting global senior pastors in Houston’s absence. In March 2022, Houston permanently stepped down as global senior pastor and from the board after an internal investigation found he had breached the church’s moral code of conduct by engaging in inappropriate behaviour with women in the 2010s. Two weeks after this scandal, nine of the 16 Hillsong churches in the United States announced they were leaving the global network. In August 2022, Hillsong was sued by an Australian whistleblower alleging it moved millions of dollars overseas to avoid the Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission (ACNC), with claims of large cash gifts to Houston and his family using tax-free money. In August 2023, Brian Houston was acquitted of covering up his father’s crimes. According to a 2024 census, Hillsong has 28 churches in Australia and 27 countries. The church had 100,000 people in 14 countries in September 2015, increasing to 130,000 in 21 countries by 2019. Due to the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020, the church began measuring online attendees, averaging 444,000 per weekend. Hillsong is described as a "global corporate brand" and "Australia's most powerful brand," with growth driven by large conferences, music popularity, charismatic leadership, Hillsong Television, messaging, social media, merchandising, and "health and wealth" teachings. The church is governed by the Hillsong Global Board and the Hillsong Eldership, headed by Pastors Phil and Lucinda Dooley since 2022. The elders lead spiritually, while the board manages corporate administration with one-year terms renewable. The founders, Brian and Bobbie Houston, were the global senior pastors. Brian Houston was chairman of the board until his resignation in January 2022; since 2021, Steve Crouch has been chairman of the Hillsong Global board, the husband of Donna Crouch and former accountant to the church. George Aghajanian is general manager and director of Hillsong Church Australia and its international entities. Hillsong has a global presence in Australia, Indonesia, the Philippines, Japan, many European countries, Canada, the US, South Africa, and Latin America (Argentina, Brazil, Mexico, Uruguay) as of February 2022. Its ministries include Hillsong Music, Hillsong Kids, Hillsong Youth, Hillsong Sisterhood, Hillsong Men, Hillsong Conference, Hillsong CityCare, Hillsong International Leadership College, TBN Inspire (branded as Hillsong Channel from June 2016 to 31 December 2021), TV & Film, Hillsong Performing Arts Academy, and Hillsong Health Centre, with total facilities valued at around A$100 million. The Hillsong International Leadership College originated from the Sydney and Hills Christian Life Centres. The Sydney college began in 1983 as the International Institute for Creative Ministries (IICM), moved to the Wesley Centre in 1989, became Wesley Institute (now Excelsia College), and in 1990 Robert Fergusson became principal, shifting focus to practical ministry training. In 1988, Hills CLC developed a training arm under Ian Fuller, initially called Power Ministry School, then Power Ministry College, and in 1993 the Hillsong School and School of Music were established. In 1996, after Mark Hopkins took over, the Hillsong School and School of Music were merged into the Hills Leadership College. In 1999, after the merger of Sydney CLC and Hills CLC, the Sydney college merged with the Hills Leadership College to form Hillsong International Leadership College, with Duncan Corby appointed principal of its City campus. It was approved as a registered training organisation in December 2002, with around 900 full-time students by 2007, mostly from overseas. In February 2016, Duncan Corby was dean and Catrina Henderson was principal; by late 2016, the name was shortened to Hillsong College, with campuses in Sydney and Phoenix, Arizona, and an online curriculum as of 2022. The official trading name of the city campus is Sydney Christian Life Centre Pty Ltd, and one of its tax-deductible charitable funds is the International Institute for Creative Ministries Library Trust Fund. Bobbie Houston has been especially influential in Hillsong's Sisterhood ministry for women, mentoring many women leaders. While the church supports traditional roles of wife and mother, it asserts that its ministries "empower" women, increasing their choices in sexuality and child rearing, encouraging small business and workplace promotions, and promoting women’s participation in cultural events and religious teaching. The Sisterhood addresses issues such as HIV/AIDS, domestic violence, and human trafficking, with midweek gatherings for women and a Thursday meeting for mothers, including businesswomen, and quarterly "Sisterhood United" meetings for working women. Members describe Bobbie’s authority as stemming from a Pentecostal understanding of Spirit empowerment. Hillsong has multiple campuses in New South Wales, including Baulkham Hills, two Sydney city campuses (one at the original Sydney CLC site), several suburbs, and one each in Newcastle and Wollongong, with one or two churches in major cities across other states except South Australia. It has churches in 30 countries and reported 150,000 regular attendees globally as of February 2022. In 2020, Hillsong purchased the heritage-listed Avalon Theatre in Hobart for $2.55 million, which underwent renovations in 2022. In 1986, Hillsong established CityCare in New South Wales, offering community services including personal development, counselling, a health centre, and youth mentoring, with "street teams" caring for the homeless. In July 2008, concerns were raised about the Hillsong CityCare Shine program for girls in public schools, community groups, and the juvenile justice system, with critics claiming it was inappropriate, reinforced gender stereotypes, and taught girls to be attractive to men. Hillsong stated parents were supportive and the program broke down barriers, denied it was used for evangelism, but a teacher’s federation representative insisted children were exposed to religious content. Hillsong was formerly affiliated with the Australian Christian Churches (Assemblies of God in Australia), and its beliefs are evangelical and charismatic. The church holds diverse positions on non-central doctrines, including opposition to abortion and support for teaching creationism and intelligent design in schools. Hillsong's prosperity teachings have been criticized by Christian leaders Tim Costello and George Pell, though Costello later expressed satisfaction with changes made by Brian Houston and wrote a foreword to Hillsong’s 2019 annual report. Peter Costello, Tim Costello’s brother and former Australian Treasurer, has defended the church against unorthodoxy accusations. Hillsong has been described by music scholar Tom Wagner as a "confluence of sophisticated marketing techniques and popular music," with Hillsong United and Hillsong Worship driving global popularity. The church has produced over 40 albums, selling over 11 million copies, including Hillsong Kids for children. Hillsong Chapel features acoustic arrangements, quieter than the typical electric guitar, keyboard, and drums. Albums have achieved gold status in Australia, with "People Just Like Us" reaching platinum. The 2004 live album For All You've Done reached No. 1 on the ARIA charts. In September 2012, Hillsong released The Global Project, a collection of popular songs in nine languages: Spanish, Portuguese, Korean, Mandarin, Indonesian, German, French, Swedish, and Russian. The Hillsong Worship albums, previously led by Darlene Zschech and Reuben Morgan and known as Hillsong Live before 2010, have been widely influential in Pentecostal and Evangelical churches, with many worship expressions such as raised hands, vocal utterance, and dance being adopted in Evangelical services.

"Hillsong's worship music, which became an early hit in the mid-1990s with the song "To the Lord," has had a broad influence in both Pentecostal and Evangelical churches, with many of its worship expressions—such as raised hands, vocal utterance, and dance—being adopted in Evangelical services. Hillsong Music has released over 40 albums since 1992, many achieving gold status in Australia, with one, *People Just Like Us*, reaching platinum status. The 2004 live praise and worship album *For All You've Done* reached No. 1 on the mainstream Australian album charts (ARIA). In 2008, Reuben Morgan became Hillsong's third worship leader. The Hillsong Worship albums, previously known as Hillsong Live before 2014 and led by Darlene Zschech and Reuben Morgan, all achieved gold status in Australia and were recorded at the Sydney campus(es), edited and produced by Hillsong Music Australia. The series began as a compilation of songs and evolved into studio-recorded albums. To increase mainstream visibility, Hillsong signed an agreement with Warner Music Australia in 1999 and later with Sony Music Australia in 2003. In 2018, Hillsong Worship won its first Grammy Award for Best Contemporary Christian Music Performance/Song for "What a Beautiful Name." Hillsong United, conceived as the youth arm of the worship ministry, produced annual live albums with a focus on alternative rock and later transitioned into a band with an eleven-member fixed lineup, emphasizing studio albums. Their song "Oceans (Where Feet May Fail)" was No. 1 on the Billboard Hot Christian Songs list for a full year, reached No. 1 on the Billboard Christian Songs chart in 2014 and 2016, No. 2 in 2015, and was named the No. 1 song of the 2010s decade. The New York Times described their music as "ornate mainstream arena rock but with God-only lyrics that are vetted for adherence to theology." Joel Houston, Hillsong's creative director and former lead pastor of Hillsong New York, leads Hillsong United. Hillsong Young & Free was established in 2012 as a youth branch targeting postmillennial youth, featuring electronic dance music and was founded by Laura Toggs and Peter Toganivalu, with Toggs resigning in 2023. Hillsong Kids produces music for children, with *Jesus Is My Superhero* and *Super Strong God* included on Natalie Gillespie's "Best Christian Children's Albums" lists for 2005 and 2006, respectively. In late March 2022, Network 10 removed Hillsong-produced television programs from its schedule and 10Play due to controversies involving Brian Houston, who resigned as senior pastor after being indicted in a misconduct investigation. Brian Houston announced through X that he would launch a new church in 2024 via an online platform. On 9 March 2016, Trinity Broadcasting Network (TBN) partnered with Hillsong, rebranding its digital sub-channel, The Church Channel, as the broadcast version of Hillsong Channel on 1 June 2016, and the American linear channel as TBN Inspire on 1 January 2022, with international versions following in April 2022; Hillsong remained a partner. Due to scandals involving Brian Houston, TBN removed Hillsong Channel and replaced it with non-pulpit teachings, worship programs, documentaries, and a one-hour flagship program. Hillsong Conference, first held in 1986 and now the largest annual conference in Australia as of January 2022, takes place in Sydney, London, and New York City each year, hosted by Brian and Bobbie Houston, with global guests. The 2011 conference was described by Baptist minister Michael Frost as having an "electric, almost carnival atmosphere." The 2014 New York event was held at Madison Square Garden, and the London conference was held at The O2 Arena over three days, continuing at that venue until at least 2018. On 16 September 2016, the documentary *Hillsong: Let Hope Rise*, directed by Michael John Warren and previously set for release in April 2015, was released in U.S. cinemas after being acquired by Pure Flix Entertainment; it explores Hillsong's rise and focuses on Hillsong United's songwriting and performance at The Forum in Inglewood, California. In 2022–2023, several media programs examined Hillsong's rise and fall: Discovery+ released *Hillsong: A Megachurch Exposed* in March 2022, revealing allegations of child-sex crimes, marital affairs, and mishandling of congregant funds; in March 2023, The Betoota Advocate partnered with Paramount to release a satirical series including a Hillsong episode; The Herald Sun produced an investigative podcast, *Faith on Trial*; and in June 2023, ex-Hillsong member Marc Fennell presented *The Kingdom* on SBS Television. On 19 May 2023, Hulu released a four-part documentary series, *The Secrets of Hillsong*, in the U.S. and Australia, directed by Stacy Lee and produced by Scout Productions and Vanity Fair Studios, covering scandals in Australia and the U.S., including interviews with former congregants, journalists, and former pastors Carl and Laura Lentz. The series begins with Carl Lentz's efforts to build a revival in New York through Hillsong NYC, which opened on 17 October 2010, quickly becoming a megachurch attracting celebrities like Justin Bieber, the Kardashian-Jenner family, Selena Gomez, Vanessa Hudgens, Kyrie Irving, and Jay-Z. By 2020, the church's reputation declined, and Carl Lentz's Instagram post about being unfaithful to his wife of 17 years sparked public backlash. Former congregants reported allegations of racism, sexual abuse, homophobia, and being exploited for free services. The series reveals that Frank Houston, the founder of Sydney Christian Life Centre and father of Brian Houston, sexually abused boys in the 1960s and 1970s, with one victim being abused from age 7 to 12; in 1999, his mother reported the abuse to the Assemblies of God, but Brian Houston, then national president, allegedly failed to report it. Brian Houston claimed it was reasonable not to report when the victim was an adult and did not want the crime exposed, a claim denied by the victim. The victim testified before the Royal Commission into Institutional Responses to Child Sexual Abuse that Frank Houston offered him AU$10,000 at a McDonald's in the presence of Nabi Saleh. Frank Houston eventually confessed during an internal investigation and was found to have abused children in New Zealand; he resigned in 2000 and was merged into Hillsong Church. An internal investigation by Assemblies of God Australia and New Zealand found six additional credible allegations. On 5 August 2021, NSW Police issued a warrant for Brian Houston to appear in court on 5 October, alleging he concealed his father's child sexual abuse; Houston was in the U.S. at the time and denied the charges, with his lawyer stating he would plead not guilty. Houston resigned from the Hillsong board in September 2021 and temporarily stepped down from church leadership in January 2022, introducing new leaders Phil and Lucinda Dooley. In August 2023, Brian Houston was found not guilty of covering up his father's sex crimes. Hillsong has faced criticism for its stance on homosexuality, considering homosexual practice sinful and barring homosexuals from leadership roles; in February 2019, it issued a statement saying it was inclusive, though Houston previously said Hillsong accepted those who did not follow a "homosexual lifestyle." In 2014, Houston expressed greater understanding of homosexuals, later clarifying that he did not diminish biblical truth or support gay marriage. Hillsong has been criticized for its involvement with Mercy Ministries, an evangelical charity with anti-abortion and conservative views on homosexuality; the church praised Mercy Ministries' work and stated it is not involved in operational aspects, saying it has helped young women in difficult situations. Mercy Ministries in Australia was shut down on 31. Hillsong has attracted support from high-profile Australian politicians, including Prime Minister John Howard, who met with Brian Houston in 1998 and attended a Hillsong event in 2002, and Treasurer Peter Costello, who spoke at conferences in 2004 and 2005; Mark Latham declined an invitation in 2004, while Premier Bob Carr attended in 2005. Liberal MP Alan Cadman and Family First Party senate candidates Joan Woods and Ivan Herald were featured in a Hillsong circular during an election, with members asked to pray for them. Hillsong's political involvement has been questioned by media and Christian leaders, and the church has distanced itself from advocating specific parties, including Family First. Brian Houston responded by distinguishing between the church's political involvement and individual Christians' engagement. In 2005, Central Magazine reported Hillsong donated A$600 to Member of the Legislative Council Kristina Keneally for a fundraising dinner, despite Hillsong's corporate governance policy stating it does not make financial contributions to or align with political candidates. A Hillsong staff member, Maria Ieroianni, said no donation was made and the dinner was not a fundraiser; Hillsong denied the donation on its website. Keneally described the dinner as a fundraiser, and the NSW Electoral Commission records confirm this. In 2005, Hillsong was accused of misusing government grants—reportedly spending A$40 million in 2004 and A$50 million in 2010—and in 2005, it was accused of using grant funds for its own staff salaries, including A$80,000 for Hillsong Emerge CEO Leigh Coleman, who had no direct involvement in the programs. One microloan program paid A$315,000 to Hillsong staff over a year, though only six loans averaging A$2,856 were granted. Hillsong listed RACA as a co-funder, but RACA denied ever providing funding. In 2006, Hillsong was stripped of A$414,000 for faking Indigenous endorsement; it was also accused of offering RACA A$280,000 to silence complaints, which they declined; a spokesperson said the offer was not meant to silence but to amicably resolve the issue. Pushes for a charity commission in Australia have arisen due to claims that religious organizations like Hillsong avoid taxes by paying staff in tax-exempt fringe benefits. In 2010, The Sunday Telegraph reported the Houston family enjoyed a lavish lifestyle, almost entirely tax-free, including vehicles and expense accounts. In early 2023, 153 staff members accepted voluntary redundancies in 2022, reportedly saving the church nearly $10 million, following accusations of extravagant spending and fraud, alongside an independent review into the church's financial structure. Hillsong does not allow homosexuals to assume leadership roles, though it issued a statement in February 2019 claiming inclusivity; previously, Brian Houston had stated that Hillsong would accept individuals who did not follow a "homosexual lifestyle." In 2014, Houston expressed greater understanding of homosexuals, but later clarified his position after facing criticism from some Christians for allegedly supporting homosexuality, stating in a website message that he had not diminished biblical truth or suggested Hillsong supported gay marriage. The church has faced criticism for its involvement with Mercy Ministries, an evangelical charity with anti-abortion views and a conservative stance on homosexuality; Hillsong praised Mercy's work and claimed it was not involved in operational aspects, noting that the organization had helped young women in difficult situations, though Mercy Ministries in Australia closed on 31 October 2009 due to financial challenges and declining support. Former member Tanya Levin criticized Hillsong in her book, describing its governance as authoritarian, lacking financial accountability, resistant to free thought, and lacking compassion, calling it "toxic Christianity" in an interview with Andrew Denton. Many former members accused the church of exploiting volunteers through overwork, lack of recognition, and interference in privacy. In 2008, Michael Guglielmucci, a pastor of Planetshakers Church, composed a song about his cancer, which was included in Hillsong's album This Is Our God; he later admitted to lying about his illness, and Hillsong leadership said they were unaware and that he was seeking help, with the Australian Christian Churches promising to return or donate donations inspired by the song; "Healer" was subsequently removed from future releases. In 2015, Mark Driscoll was invited to attend the Hillsong annual conference but was removed after offensive comments about women were revealed, though a pre-recorded interview with him was played during the event. Gary Clarke, then pastor of Hillsong London, faced criticism for refusing to comment on George Floyd’s murder, stating on 30 May 2020 that addressing it as a pastor from another country would not help; both Clarke and Houston apologized, and in early 2021, Clarke and his wife Cathy were moved to an international leadership role. In June 2020, Hillsong publicly supported Black Lives Matter, with Brian Houston stating the church was committed to ending racism and affirming that "black lives matter" until that goal was achieved. The church held a panel discussion featuring people of colour, including Robyn Ober, pastor of Hillsong Darwin and an Aboriginal Australian academic. Carl Lentz led Hillsong’s first U.S. church in New York City in 2010 and became friends with Justin Bieber, building a celebrity following; under his leadership, the East Coast expansion became focused on fashion and serving pastors and patrons, with volunteers reportedly working long hours, being treated as second-class citizens, and gaslighted; around 2017, two volunteers who raised concerns about Lentz were allegedly intercepted and dismissed. In 2020, Lentz was fired after it was found he had engaged in more than one extra-marital affair and was currently involved in one; his lover stated Hillsong is a "money machine" and that Lentz was a victim of the church. In early 2021, Vanity Fair, the Christian Post, and News.com.au reported that Anna Crenshaw, a student at Hillsong Leadership College, was indecently assaulted by Jason Mays, a married Hillsong administrator and son of the church’s director of human resources; Mays pleaded guilty in January 2020 to indecent assault, received two years probation and mandatory counselling, and was banned for 12 months before being reinstated to ministry and volunteering at worship services. Crenshaw criticized leadership for downplaying the incident and not holding Mays accountable; Brian Houston later apologized for a tweet questioning Crenshaw’s account. In the same month, several students wrote a letter criticizing leadership for allowing Mays to remain on staff. In September 2021, 60 Minutes aired a segment titled "Hillsong Hell" featuring Crenshaw and a woman known as "Katherine," who alleged she was raped by a fellow church member in 2018 on church premises; both women claimed Hillsong ignored their complaints and downplayed the incidents. Hillsong responded by calling the report "factually wrong, sensationalised, unbalanced and highly unethical," stating it had investigated both cases, reported the assault on Crenshaw to police in May 2019, and defended retaining Mays, citing the magistrate’s description of the offence as "low-level," Mays’s remorse, and contradictions in Crenshaw’s account; it also claimed "Katherine" refused to provide details or report to police. Nine News journalist Tom Steinfort criticized Hillsong’s response as "tone-deaf" and accused leadership of victim blaming. In January 2022, during the pandemic, a Hillsong youth camp at Glenrock near Newcastle was filmed dancing and singing without masks, violating public health orders; the NSW Premier expressed shock, and Hillsong apologized, stating it would comply with health orders and maintained the event was not a music festival; police spoke with organizers but declined to fine them; all attendees were tested before arrival. In March 2022, Brian Houston resigned as global senior pastor after an internal investigation found he had engaged in inappropriate behavior with women connected to the church in both 2013 and 2019. In January 2021, Hillsong Dallas pastor Reed Bogard resigned, two weeks before an investigation found he had raped a female junior colleague between 2013 and 2014, with Hillsong Australia aware of the affair by late 2014 but choosing not to act; the Dallas campus was paused in April 2021. On 24 March 2022, Sam Collier, the lead pastor of Hillsong Atlanta, resigned, citing ongoing scandals and allegations against senior figures, and announced plans to start his own church; he was the first African-American pastor to lead a Hillsong church. In late March 2022, Terry Crist, lead pastor of Hillsong Phoenix, announced his church would leave the global network due to loss of confidence in the Global Board leadership following Houston’s resignation. As of 6 April 2022, nine Hillsong branches in the U.S. had separated from the church after revelations about Houston. On 10 May 2023, Houston’s daughter Laura Toggs and her husband Peter Toganivalu, founders of Hillsong Young & Free, announced they were leaving the church, citing a divine calling elsewhere. Several worship leaders, including Toggs, Brooke Ligertwood, Taya Gaukrodger, and Benjamin William Hastings, have since departed. An ABC TV 7.30 report on 6 April 2022 revealed Hillsong had acquired numerous properties through a network of entities worldwide, including taking control of Garden City Church in 2009, transferring over 12 Brisbane properties to a Hillsong charity without money, taking over finances of a Sydney church that later left, and taking control of Hillsong Kyiv in 2014 by coercing pastors to hand over assets and leave. An investigator from the Trinity Foundation found Hillsong owned at least three New York City condominiums, a $3.5-million home in California, and 31 Arizona properties, expected to be worth $40 million by 2023; its complex corporate and financial structure provides protection from litigation demanding large payouts. On 19 March 2022, John Mays, head of people and development, wrote to global leadership recommending dismissal of the Houstons, citing their contribution to "many unhealthy people practices over many years," claiming Brian Houston had a "strong, immovable, leadership disposition together with a distinct lack of personal accountability," and that Bobbie shared responsibility for accountability; he stated his motive was to support employees, not personal malice, and expressed appreciation for aspects of the Houstons’ legacy.
